hook.en: An accountant builds a depreciation schedule once. Next year the cost of the machine changes, and every figure in the schedule updates by itself. That is the power of a spreadsheet.

objectives.en: Explain cells, formulas and cell references
Use common functions (SUM, AVERAGE, IF, ROUND, MIN, MAX)
Prepare accounting schedules such as depreciation and payroll in a spreadsheet

narration.en: An accountant builds a depreciation schedule once. Next year the cost of the machine changes, and every figure in the schedule updates by itself. That is the power of a spreadsheet.

body.en: A spreadsheet is a grid of rows (numbered) and columns (lettered); each cell has an address such as B5. A cell may hold text, a number or a formula, which starts with an equals sign, for example =B5*$B$2. A relative reference (B5) changes when the formula is copied to another row; an absolute reference ($B$2) stays fixed, which is used for a rate or a constant. A mixed reference fixes only the row or the column. Copying one formula down a column builds a whole schedule.

points.en: Cell address: column letter + row number

body.en: Functions are ready-made formulas: SUM adds a range, AVERAGE finds the mean, MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest values, ROUND rounds to given places, and IF chooses between two results by a condition, for example =IF(C5>40000, C5*10%, 0) for a bonus. Spreadsheets are used for depreciation schedules, payroll (basic pay, allowances, deductions and net pay), loan repayment tables, ratio analysis, and preparing a trial balance or comparative statements from ledger balances. Charts show the results graphically.

problem.en: A machine costs ₹2,00,000 (cell B1) and is depreciated at 20% (cell B2) by the written down value method. Write the depreciation formula for year 1 (opening value in B5) and find depreciation for years 1 to 3.

steps.en: Formula in C5: =B5*$B$2; closing value D5: =B5-C5; next opening B6: =D5.

answer.en: Depreciation ₹40,000, ₹32,000 and ₹25,600; the formula =B5*$B$2 is copied down.
